bottom_line.native_faults: Japan/7 and India/7: 0xc0000005 inside ntdll.dll 10.0.26100.7920, 16.76 s apart, at unrelated simulated dates (2031-01, 2024-12).
bottom_line.supported_medium_confidence: Long-lived D: handles failed (D: is recorded in 28 Sep notes as the external USB drive) while new D: handles worked; the frozen runner turns the failed journal write into halt_children -> Popen.kill -> TerminateProcess(handle,1) (two exit-1 workers), the failed stderr into exit 120, and the verifier event write into Errno 13. Inference: the journal entry itself was lost, and the accepted journal-diagnosis record (S25/preparation/journal-diagnosis-20261001/README.md) does not attribute the exit-1s to the kill path.
bottom_line.not_supported: In-process causes: deterministic sim defect, stack overflow and Rust OOM abort are contradicted by the exit signature; heap corruption is unsupported and does not by itself explain cross-process timing.
bottom_line.plausible_not_established: A shared host-level event at ~23:28 UTC (~0.16% chance if the two fault times were independent and uniform over the 20,755 s four-worker window). Neither commit exhaustion nor the USB D: failure is shown to produce 0xc0000005 in ntdll.

hypotheses.title: Deterministic simulation/logic defect at a specific simulated state
hypotheses.reason: Safe-Rust defects in this release build end as Err/panic (stderr, result.json failure, exit 101), 0xc00000fd or 0xc0000409, never a silent 0xc0000005 in ntdll; faults 17 s apart at unrelated simulated dates. Residual variants (deep recursion; undefined behaviour in std or a dependency) are rows 2 and 4, which is why the evidence lens rated it unsupported rather than disproven.

hypotheses.title: Stack exhaustion
hypotheses.reason: Expected 0xc00000fd plus "has overflowed its stack"; observed 0xc0000005 and 0-byte stderr; JSON depth 13 (Linux snapshots 1991-1995) vs serde_json limit 128; Linux test-thread stack 116 KiB of 2 MiB (continuous to 1990-04-01, point readings to 1995-02).

hypotheses.title: Rust allocation failure (OOM abort)
hypotheses.reason: Expected "memory allocation of N bytes failed" plus 0xc0000409 in the exe (Linux control reproduced message + SIGABRT); observed 0xc0000005 at two different ntdll offsets.

hypotheses.title: Heap corruption via unsafe code in std/dependencies (serde_json, itoa, memchr, zmij) or miscompile
hypotheses.reason: Not excluded by the exit code (undetected NT-heap damage can fault in ntdll), but no dump, unresolved offsets, valgrind clean (one Linux month); does not explain two processes 17 s apart or the Python-side failures.

hypotheses.title: Worker memory as contributor
hypotheses.reason: Workers are large (Linux VmHWM 1.50 GiB by 1994) but wave 1 ran four workers through the larger 2008-2014 state without fault; no crash-time memory data.

hypotheses.title: Host commit/memory exhaustion at ~23:28
hypotheses.reason: No 23:28 commit sample (7.94-8.15 GiB headroom measured 3.5-4 h later); known exhaustion paths give 0xc0000409/0xc00000fd/0xc0000006; a concurrent rustc release build survived; Python errors were EACCES not MemoryError.

hypotheses.title: Unbounded simulated-state growth
hypotheses.standing: unsupported (contradicted by size data; not adversarially reviewed)
hypotheses.reason: Archives stay between 116.6 and 186.7 MB after 1994, peak ~2010; crash-time 126.8-133.5 MB = 0.71-0.73 of each process's own survived peak.

hypotheses.title: windows-gnu unwinding/TLS path faulting in ntdll
hypotheses.reason: No panic message; catch_unwind recorded nothing; symbolizing the offsets would test it.

hypotheses.title: Shared host-level event at ~23:28
hypotheses.reason: Two independent processes faulted 16.76 s apart (~0.16% if fault times were independent and uniform over the four-worker window); every candidate mechanism lacks direct evidence.

hypotheses.title: D: handle failure -> evidence loss and runner kill chain
hypotheses.reason: Long-open D: handles failed (runner journal, launcher stdout/stderr, verifier events.jsonl) while new D: handles worked; frozen runner/verifier code explains exit 1 x2, exit 120 and Errno 13. Win32 error unknown; "device not ready" plausible not shown; onset bounded only to after 17:43 (evidence lens: a D: build ran 23:19:04-23:36:50 successfully, so a volume event more likely preceded 23:19).

hypotheses.title: Same D: event caused the native faults
hypotheses.reason: A failed page-in of the D:-mapped image is 0xc0000006, even inside ntdll; the other two workers on the same image kept running until killed.

hypotheses.title: Hardware fault or injected third-party module
hypotheses.standing: open (no evidence either way; not adversarially reviewed)
hypotheses.reason: No WHEA, security-product or loaded-module evidence collected.

verdict_flag_note: Reviewers applied refuted=true both to contradicted and (default rule) to unsupported hypotheses; standings above separate these.

key_facts.fact: Both native faults are 0xc0000005 in ntdll.dll 10.0.26100.7920 (module timestamp 0x5ffc11eb): Japan/7 PID 0x9150 offset 0x166167 at 23:28:41.129Z; India/7 PID 0x4B98 offset 0x10579 at 23:28:57.885Z.

Executable, runner journal, launcher logs and verifier lived under D:\spheres-offload, which the 28 Sep records identify as the external USB drive (inferred from paths there, not stated outright).
Leader-art release compile (attempt-02) ran 23:19:04 to ~23:31:21 on the same machine and its tests passed.

Canonical state peaks 175.4-186.7 MB around 2010 in every cell; crash/kill-time 126.8-133.5 MB (0.71-0.73 of own peak). Summed four-worker state ~541 MB at the fault vs ~709 MB estimated wave-1 peak (uniform-pace assumption); alternatives: 526.7 MB summing each wave-2 cell's last checkpoint, 725.8 MB wave-1 peak with cells aligned by simulated date (2010-04-01).
No unsafe code in spheres-sim/src, spheres-web/src or vendored tiny_http (forbid(unsafe_code)) at 68ba0622; dependencies serde_json, itoa, memchr, zmij contain unsafe.
